en: A certain person, afflicted by separation from a beloved and inflamed by the fire of grief, having exerted effort to maintain fortitude, addresses his own mind as follows: (1)
Why do you lament over that person who, having entered upon the path of action, went there without being summoned and without fault?
If death were to befall him alone and no one else, it would be right to cry out loudly; for this is indeed a great humiliation. (3)
Now, since death stands before every being that is born,
you ought not to grieve upon seeing this common calamity.
Out of greed for union with a beloved, a person is consumed by grief,
just as a yak is consumed by a forest fire within the depths of the woods due to its greed for its tail-hair.
Since everyone must eventually depart wherever they have gone,
why is grief felt for one who has already departed long ago?
Truly, these creatures are heedless before Death, whose rod is most terrible;
they stand facing him like a doe before a lion in the forest seeking to kill her. (7)
When there is no remedy for that which must die by any means whatsoever, why do you maintain your fortitude, like a fish pulled out from the water? (8)
Have you ever seen, heard of, or even suspected anyone—whether on earth or in heaven—who was born and would not die? (9)
This entire triple world is consumed by the fire of impermanence, just as a flowering forest is set ablaze by a forest fire. 10.
Even living beings from the peak of existence, perverted by the notion of permanence, are dragged away by the noose of death like great elephants by a snare. (11)
Even Brahmā, having enjoyed the bliss born of meditation,
is cast down from his celestial abode by impermanence, just as the bank of a river is eroded by water.
Thousands of Purandaras and hundreds of Cakravartins have been extinguished by Time, like lamps by the wind. (13)
Even though the great seers possessed the five superknowledges, they were unable to go further into the distant sky to that place which is beyond the reach of death.
Where the earth is consumed by fire and even Mount Meru is shattered, where the waters of the ocean dry up—what need is there to speak of the body? 15.
If even the Buddhas, whose bodies possess the essence of a diamond, are subject to impermanence, what concern can there be for other embodied beings, who are like the pith of a plantain tree? (16)
A living being is carried away by death, even while embraced by kinsmen, just as a serpent in the depths of the ocean is seized by Garuḍa. 17.
"Alas, world of living beings! Alas, beloved!"—thus crying out most piteously, the world is swallowed by death, just as a frog is swallowed by a serpent. (18)
Indeed, without having reached the far shore of its difficult-to-cross duties, this world enters the mouth of Death, just as a ship enters the abode of sea-monsters. 19.
When someone departs for the next world, no one follows them;
in that state, one becomes indistinguishable, whether they were hated or beloved. (20)
Having conceived affection for others under the notion that they are one's own kin,
a person sinks into the mire of desire, just as an elephant sinks into a great morass.
As many relatives as have been gained and lost by you in saṃsāra,
they truly do not equal even the grains of sand in the Ganges.
He whom you cherished with such effort, regarding him as a son, is that very same person who, separated by another birth, has been struck down, regarded as an enemy. (23)
Those very breasts that were sucked by you from your own kinsmen in another life—having killed them, their blood was drunk and their flesh was eaten. (24)
Whoever may be your husband, even if worshipped by you with your head hundreds of times, he alone shall become your slave, struck by you with your foot hundreds of times. (25)
A person is seen in one way at first and changes into another through the influence of causes,
just like the host of the Seven Sages.
Just as raindrops falling in the sky scatter upon meeting [the wind], so too do living beings perish in saṃsāra after having come together. 27.
In this world, the meeting and parting of embodied beings occurs in a mere moment, like logs floating upon a river whose current is turbulent. (28)
Oh, the power of delusion, by which the world is so bewildered that, forgetting the suffering of separation, it forms attachments to union! (29)
There is no stage whatsoever that is devoid of the Pure Abodes, where beings do not perform their drama through the diverse costumes of karma. (30)
The amount of molten copper that has been drunk again and again in the hells is such that even the waters in all the oceans do not equal its measure. (31)
And that act of eating excrement committed while in the state of a dog or a boar would be greater in measure than Mount Meru, the king of mountains. || 32 ||
And as for the tears shed in saṃsāra due to separation from kinsmen—even the ocean would not be a sufficient vessel for those drops of tears from their eyes. (33)
The heap of heads that were severed by one another for the sake of food is higher than and surpasses even the world of Brahmā.
The dust that was devoured here by hungry worms has been sufficient to fill the great ocean of milk.
Having heard of that most terrible suffering from hunger and thirst experienced in the world of the hungry ghosts (pretas), what person of feeling would not even give away their own flesh? (36)
I am unable to describe the humiliation I have experienced among men through the fault of poverty; my tongue seems as if it were ashamed. (37)
Having long experienced happiness on the surface of the celestial vault,
the denizens of heaven remain unsatiated by divine sense-objects, like fires with dry wood.
Furthermore, when their life-span has ended, they fall from the triple heaven to the earth like birds whose wings have been clipped, once their meritorious karma is exhausted. (39)
Since this world revolves like a wheel, impelled by karma, therefore one should abandon attachment and fix the mind upon liberation. (40)
